title: The Art of Letting Go
author: Krista Stevens
content:
For The American Scholar, Lisa Russ Spaar offers us beautiful litany of loss in all its various shapes and forms. From those we love to objects like keys, from our teeth to our moral compass, Spaar takes a close look at what we go through when we experience loss at various times in our lives, and how losses tend to stack up as we age.

I’ve informally polled several friends, colleagues, and family members about their first remembered losses. For most, it was when a milk tooth fell out, usually around the age of six. (Surely there are primal reasons many of us dream throughout our lifetimes about our teeth, as important as they are to speaking, eating.) More than 20 years ago, one of my talented undergraduates, Molly, wrote a poem about losing her first tooth while sledding in winter. Upon tonguing the little bloody socket that remained, she wrote, “I taste my death.” That line has haunted me over the decades. Again, our bodies: made for loss. Language: our ability to articulate what that might mean.

I often wonder what was happening in my late mother’s mind as she sank, over a period of 10-plus years, into the tangled ambages of dementia. She lost the names of things and people. She lost any memory of who we were, those of us who cared for her, even her devoted husband, my father. She finally even forgot that she was not only an alcoholic with a fifth of Scotch hidden in the breadbox but also a chain smoker, though she’d occasionally hold a drinking straw to her lips and take a long, deep drag.

title: The Ledger and the Blade
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
In 1993, an audience member at the Citizen Cup tennis tournament stabbed Monica Seles, then a 19-year-old phenom who was then dethroned from the top of the world tennis rankings. The attack, writes Terrence Doyle, “was a physical manifestation of a logic that has since become our default: the idea that an athlete is not a human to be witnessed, but a data point to be managed, edited, or deleted.” I briefly mentioned Doyle’s disturbing essay a week ago, but it has stayed with me since: a worrying meditation on the ease with which athletes are abstracted into mere data sets. It deserves your deeper consideration.

Perhaps the most profound shift is the collapse of our ability to trust what we see. In 1993, we had the tape. We saw Parche reach over the rail and thrust his blade into Seles’ back. We agreed on the wound. Today, that on-the-ground truth is being eroded. We’re being told by powerful forces to disregard the evidence of our own senses—to see every physical trauma as a narrative threat or a potential deepfake.

What’s all that racket? A few features from the world of tennis

Can Andre Agassi Enjoy Pickleball More Than He Hated Tennis?

Lizzy Goodman | The New York Times Magazine | September 7, 2026 | 5,478 words

“After years of relative quiet, the public is meeting ‘Andre 2.0’ — a pickleball booster, an open book and a guy eager to build a less tortured relationship with competition.”

‘I’m Good, I Promise’: The Loneliness of the Low-Ranking Tennis Player

Conor Niland | The Guardian | June 27, 2024 | 3,845 words

“I was once Ireland’s No 1 player, and tried for years to climb the global ranks. But life at the bottom of the top can be brutal.”

The Unbearable Greatness of Djokovic

Scott Stossel | The Atlantic | May 28, 2024 | 4,580 words

“Novak Djokovic may be the greatest tennis player ever—and I can’t stand him.”

title: Nvidia ensure unboxing a ludicrously expensive new graphics card isn't limited to real life in these RAM crisis times by releasing a GeForce 8800 GTX unpacking sim
author: Mark Warren
content:
Hey at least the card in this bit of 2006 nostalgia bait has only cost you a virtual arm and leg

In what feels a fairly cheeky move during a time when memory shortages have infamously made it pretty much impossible to buy a decently powerful new graphics card without spending approximately a gazillion pounds/dollars/dollarpounds, Nvidia have decided to put out a Steam demo that allows folks to re-live the feeling of unboxing a ludicrously expensive graphics card in 2006.

The demo, dubbed GeForce 8800 GTX - 20 Years of a Legend, has been developed by Dylan Browne. He previously made Through The Ages, a "real-time high end graphical cinematic that takes us on a nostalgic journey through three of NVIDIA's iconic GPUs" which is also on Steam for reasons.

The GeForce 8800 GTX demo, as you might've guessed, is a tribute to that specific card in the form of a tech demo simulating what it was like to unbox one in a mid-2000s bedroom. Seriously, there's a copy of Crysis on the desk so you know this is the domain of a true devotee to the best graphics available in around 2007.

"Step into a 2006-era PC gaming room, unbox the GeForce 8800 GTX, inspect it up close, and install it in an era-accurate PC tower," the demo's description declares. "Explore nods to GeForce history and hidden easter eggs as DLSS 4.5 with Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, Ray Reconstruction, path tracing, and Mega Geometry bring the nostalgic setting to life. From holding the card to the glow of the monitor, rediscover a moment in PC gaming history - or experience it for the first time!"

As the GeForce 8800 GTX was a top-line card that cost $599 on release in 2006 - about $1,000 in today's money if the online inflation calculator I've just used is on the money - this isn't really a 'we know cards are ludicrously expensive right now, but here's a reminder of when you used to be able to actually afford to unbox one' sort of demo. It is at least a free way to virtually experience having blown a chunk of your savings on something that can render really sexy textures without the existential dread of doing so in real life.

Well, I say that, I've just noticed the minimum requirements for the demo note that you'll need an RTX 4070 card. So, depending on your current setup, this might well be a case of Nvidia offering the chance to render unboxing a card you couldn't afford in 2006 via a card you can't afford in 2026.

Is that about the best we can all hope for in 2026? Probably.

title: Nintendo game sales surge thanks to Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, but Switch 2 hardware suffers big decline
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Yenning for more.

Nintendo's latest financial earnings report is here, revealing healthy software sales thanks to the enormously popular Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. Sales of Switch 2 hardware, however, are down.

As per Nintendo's 2nd Quarter fiscal earnings report, focusing on the three-month period ending 30th September 2026, Switch 2 hardware registered a big drop in sales during the first half of the current financial year (FY27).

Over that period, Nintendo sold 6.49m Switch 2 units and 1.27m units of the original Switch - equating to a 37.4 percent decline for Switch 2 and 32.7 percent decline for Switch 1 compared to the same period last year. Nintendo had previously forecast a decline in hardware sales, and the company still expects to sell 16.50m Switch 2 units by the end of the current fiscal year.

Nintendo software sales, on the other hand, saw a big year-on-year boost of 18.8 percent on Switch 2 (to 24.49m units) and a smaller increase of 6.8 percent on Switch 1. That's all thanks to the release of several popular first- and third-party titles over the first half of FY27. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream was by far the most successful game with 8.81m units sold, followed by Rhythm Heaven Groove at 2.89m. Splatoon Raiders (the only Switch 2 exclusive of the three) sold 2.42m. Nintendo also highlighted a 60.5 percent year-on-year increase in digital game sales.

The increase in software unit sales and the "continued weakness of the Yen" couldn't prevent the overall business from declining by 15.3 percent year-on-year, however.

Other remaining releases in Nintendo' s current fiscal year include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (which launches today and was awarded five stars in Eurogamer's review), Switch 2 re-releases of Pikmin 2 and Xenoblade Chronicles 3, as well as Metroid Ravenous, which arrives early in 2027.

title: Echoes of Mirror's Edge, Dishonored and a dream set in Italy I once had can be found in Boars in Rome, an expressive parkour platformer set in dystopian Rome
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
When in, well, you know

Years ago, I had this dream where I was parkouring through a greatly sunken version of Venice, no doubt sourced from the many hours I put into Assassin's Creed 2 as a teen who should have been studying for their GCSEs a lot more than they were. It's stuck with me after all this time mostly because of how much I wanted to capture that feeling again somehow, as the real Assassin's Creed didn't quite cut it. And lo and behold, there I was today browsing Bluesky when I came across Boars in Rome, a Mirror's Edge and Counter Strike Surf inspired parkour platformer set in a dystopian version of Rome.

Truthfully, witnessing the clip I've shared below was baffling to me. "This is what I dreamt of!" More or less, anyway, for the setting isn't quite the same; "You have been selected to start a new life off planet. Earth has been abandoned," explains the game's Steam page. "Machines keep working and nature claims what remains. Find out what happened while you were frozen in time by exploring the remnants of Rome where historical monuments mix with futurist megastructures."

Mirrors Edge x Counter Strike Surf where you parkour on anything! Be smooth n stylish in dystopian Rome. Or just jump around and explore, whatever works for you. It's called Boars in Rome! #PitchYaGame

[image or embed]

— Benji Savage (@ceplok.bsky.social) November 6, 2026 at 12:05 PM

Not all of it matches that dream of mine, some of it leans much more into brutalism than the typical, much older architecture you'd expect of Rome, but it's there nonetheless. In motion, Boars in Rome feels quite oneiric too. There is so much more control over the game's avatar than what my real body is capable of, or wants to do. You can run, jump, slide and wallrun, positioning it quite closely to VHOLUME mechanically. Where it differs is in its additives, movement tech like being able to swing on lampposts or vault over low down obstacles.

VHOLUME is more of a game about providing you with a simple toolkit and leaving you to push it to its maximum. Boars in Roam is a touch more expressive, and I'd dare to even call it an immersive sim. The levels you can romp around are linear, you have an end point to reach, only the journey is up to you. It certainly feels appropriate to put it in the im sim camp given that, at least the game's first level, calls to mind Viktor Antonov's work on Dishonored (and Half-Life 2, too, honestly).

As it currently stands, there's no release date for Boars in Rome, but there is a playtest you can sign up and gain immediate access to if you fancy a go yourself; you can do so on Steam right here, or at least pop it a wishlist.

title: As Xbox Helix looms, Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"
author: Kaan Serin
content:
It's been Aegis.

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

title: DOJ steps up its investigation into the Dobbs leak
author: Nora Collins
content:
Skip to main content

Newsletter

Nov 6, 2026

This week, during the first half of the November argument session, the justices heard oral arguments in four cases and quickly declined a request from the Trump administration to intervene in a voting dispute in California. However, headlines about these developments were overshadowed by Tuesday’s midterm elections. The blue wave brought new significance to debates over court reform and when Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas might retire.

At the Court This Week

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied two requests for a stay of execution from Jesse Guardado, who was sentenced to death for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone. Hours later, Guardado was executed in Florida.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

Monday morning, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by individuals who it contends are noncitizens. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since last Friday, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Looking ahead, the justices will hear arguments on Monday in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Morning Reads

Justice Dept. Steps Up Criminal Inquiry of Supreme Court Abortion Decision Leak

Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt, The New York Times

In May 2022, Politico released a leaked draft of the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the right to abortion. The leak was “a seismic breach of confidentiality” and led to “an internal inquiry by the court,” although “no leaker has ever been publicly identified.” But The New York Times reported on Thursday that the Justice Department is now “pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked” the draft opinion and that this “investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks.”

Surprise twist ricochets through Supreme Court case on AR-15 ban

John Fritze, CNN

On Thursday, defenders of “a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any ‘assault weapon or large capacity magazine,’ including AR-15 rifles,” asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a challenge to the ban that’s set to be argued in December, Viramontes v. Cook County. Attorneys for Cook County contended that the case is now moot after the “lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked [on Oct. 29] to be removed from the litigation without explanation.” Although the filings represent “a puzzling twist” in the case, “whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles,” according to CNN. That’s because Viramontes was consolidated with another case on a similar law in Connecticut, “which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut’s ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.”

Midterm Rout Closes Trump’s Window on the Supreme Court

James Romoser, The Wall Street Journal

Tuesday’s midterm elections “all but guaranteed” President Donald Trump won’t be able to put a fourth justice on the Supreme Court. Beginning in January, Democrats will have “a Senate majority—with a several-seat cushion—that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that might arise in 2027 or 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Faced with this reality, “[s]ome legal observers have floated a last-ditch scenario in which [Clarence] Thomas or [Samuel] Alito could announce their retirement in the coming days and give Trump and the outgoing Republican Senate a chance to quickly install a successor before the newly elected Congress is seated on Jan. 3.” But the Journal described this scenario as “exceedingly unlikely,” in large part because neither Alito nor Thomas appears interested in retiring. And it’s not “clear that a Supreme Court nominee could get through the lame-duck Congress even if there were a retirement, especially because some moderate Republican senators are on their way out of office and blame Trump for losing their seats.”

Senate Democrats will not let Trump put a ‘right-winger’ on the Supreme Court, Schumer vows

Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press

In a Thursday interview with the Associated Press, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said “that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put ‘a right-winger’ on the Supreme Court once they take power.” He “would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are ‘not going to allow any crappy nominees’ to be confirmed to the Supreme Court.” “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.

Democrats Can Now Fix the Supreme Court Without Reforming It

Noah Feldman, Bloomberg

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman contended that Tuesday’s election results “should cause Democrats to reconsider the wisdom of plans to pack the court or strip it of jurisdiction over certain issues.” It should no longer feel as urgent to make such changes, according to Feldman, because “[i]f a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 and the Democrats hold the Senate, the Democrats will have a chance to flip the court from 6-3 conservative to 5-4 liberal” simply by filling predicted or expected vacancies. The reform proposals floated in recent months “make little sense if Democrats take seriously the prospect of a liberal recapture of the institution,” Feldman wrote.

On Site This Week

Case Preview

Court to consider the reach of Article III courts in immigration contract dispute

By Ronald Mann

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem: Does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers?

Contributor Corner

St. Mary and the shrinking reach of Smith

By Stephanie Barclay

In her Ratio Decidendi column, Stephanie Barclay revisited Tuesday’s argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, noting that the discussion put a spotlight on 1990’s Employment Division v. Smith, a controversial ruling that made it easier for the government to overcome free exercise challenges. The ruling in St. Mary, according to Barclay, “will determine how much is left of” Smith, which has already fallen out of favor with the court.

Relist Watch

Mootness, maps, and motor vehicles

By John Elwood

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored four petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at today’s conference. Three concern a long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts and the fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

Contributor Corner

Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

By Erwin Chemerinsky

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky explored Nielsen v. Watanabe, in which the court is considering under what circumstances federal officers may be sued for money damages for constitutional violations, noting that the case comes at a time when efforts “to hold ICE agents accountable” have taken on new urgency.

Contributor Corner

Is Montgomery affirmative action’s final chapter?

By Brian Fitzpatrick

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on race and school admissions. In his AV Ristorante column on Monday, Brian Fitzpatrick explained why he believes “it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.”

Podcasts

Advisory Opinions

Legal Ramifications of a Bluenami

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the Texas Supreme Court’s blue wave, the possibility of a majority-Democrat Supreme Court, and one of the biggest Supreme Court cases of the term: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

A Closer Look

Justice Peter V. Daniel

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Peter V. Daniel, who served on the court from 1841/2 to 1860.

Like some of the other justices we’ve covered, Justice Peter V. Daniel is one that “[f]ew recall or have ever heard of.” Those who know of Daniel have not been complimentary. He has been called “a brooding proslavery fanatic” according to law professor Earl Maltz, and a 1965 book review likened him to the notoriously bigoted Justice James C. McReynolds, minus McReynolds’ occasional “charm.”

Daniel was born in April 1784 on his family’s estate in Stafford County, Virginia. After studying with private tutors and a brief stint at the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University), he read law in Richmond under Edmund Randolph, President George Washington’s attorney general and secretary of state. In 1810, Daniel married Randolph’s daughter, Lucy.

In November 1808, Daniel fought a duel in Maryland against businessman John Seddon; Seddon later died from his injuries. This did not appear to significantly slow Daniel’s career, however: He subsequently spent two one-year terms in the Virginia House of Delegates, a tenure his biographer, John P. Frank, judged as “utterly undistinguished.” In 1812, Daniel joined Virginia’s Council of State, which advised the governor, and from 1818 to 1835 served as lieutenant governor. His “friends” “apparently lacked any real warmth or affection for him, complaining of his ‘frozen deportment,’” which played out literally: In the winter of 1813, Daniel reportedly balked at spending a modest sum to keep militiamen warm, despite their officer’s warning that the men’s lives were at stake, on the reasoning that Virginia state law made the soldiers responsible for their own clothing.

Daniel’s Richmond law practice was modestly successful, but he had other aspirations. Through the Richmond Junto (a Virginia Democratic-Republican network) he organized and led the state’s Jacksonians, and, along with then-New York governor Martin Van Buren, built an “Albany-Richmond axis,” which backed Andrew Jackson for president. Daniel subsequently turned down Jackson’s offer of attorney general. In 1836, however, he accepted a federal judgeship in eastern Virginia, Jackson’s reward for his party loyalty and his support for the president’s war on the national bank.

When Justice Philip Barbour died in February 1841, Van Buren had roughly a week left in office and rushed to nominate Daniel to the court. Aware of Daniel’s reputation, Whig senators tried to stall the vote, at one point walking out together to leave the chamber without a quorum, while Democratic leaders searched the capital for their own absent senators. Daniel was ultimately confirmed 22-5 in a midnight vote. The exact date he took the oath is unclear; the Federal Judicial Center lists it in January 1842 “based on questionable authority,” while one biography entry has him joining the court in December 1841.

After he joined the bench, Daniel’s circuit assignment included Arkansas and Mississippi, which involved arduous trips from Washington. While circuit riding in 1851, for example, Daniel rode in a canal boat for two days to get from D.C. to Pittsburgh (and was not a fan of the other “vulgar and filthy” passengers).

On the court itself, close to one in three of Daniel’s written opinions was a dissent, and during his tenure, his solo dissents outnumbered any other justice’s by more than two to one. He fought against extending federal admiralty power to inland waters, and when the court did just that in 1852’s Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh, Daniel was the lone dissenter. Perhaps his best-known majority opinion came in 1848’s West River Bridge Co. v. Dix, which put Daniel opposite the famed lawyer and statesman Daniel Webster. Daniel detested Webster so much that, after meeting him, he reported his hand “was actually contaminated by contact with his.” In the case, Vermont had taken over a privately chartered toll bridge, paid compensation, and opened it as a free road, but the bridge company argued that the takeover breached the contract clause of the Constitution. Writing for the majority, Daniel held that the franchise was ordinary property that the state could take through eminent domain.

Daniel, who was a slaveholder, concurred in 1842’s Prigg v. Pennsylvania, which held that the federal Fugitive Slave Act preempted Pennsylvania’s ban on recapturing formerly enslaved persons. After Van Buren joined the antislavery Free Soilers, Daniel’s friendship with him ended, and Daniel reportedly swore he would never again set foot north of Maryland (he came to blame even bad weather on the North). In Dred Scott v. Sandford, Daniel argued that freed slaves could not be citizens because they had once been held as property and that the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (which, among many other things, had kept slavery out of land north and west of the Ohio River) was unconstitutional, thus taking a more extreme position than even Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the majority opinion.

Daniel’s first wife, Lucy, died in 1847, and his second wife died in 1857 after a candle accidentally lit her clothes on fire. Daniel died in Richmond in May 1860 following a lengthy illness. In February 1861, Republican senators blocked President James Buchanan’s pick to replace him, Jeremiah Black, making the seat one of the three vacancies that President Abraham Lincoln filled in 1862. It stayed open until July 1862, when Lincoln chose Justice Samuel Miller.

In a December 1860 memorial, the attorney general said that Daniel “held the pen of a ready writer,” but “was sometimes in danger of going too directly to his purpose and treating with too much contempt the obstacles that intervened.”

SCOTUS Quote

JUSTICE THOMAS: “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?”

MR. SCHEPERS: “In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “We're talking about now, though.”

MR. SCHEPERS: “That – we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “What about Marbury v. Madison?”

— Guerrero v. Johnson (2026)

title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
author: Lucas Ropek
content:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

title: Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s Linguistic Art
author: @NewYorker
content:
Also: Bill Irwin and Rachel Bloom in Molière, a new movie from Kogonada, the torrid post-punk of Sweeping Promises, and more.

November 6, 2026

It’s taken me some days to write about Theresa Hak Kyung Cha’s show at Artists Space, because I didn’t want to face the fact that she’s no longer around to keep growing as an artist, a thinker, and a woman. Cha explored her deep interest in language among distinct cultures—including that of her native South Korea, where she grew up, and of the United States, where she moved, in 1962, when she was eleven—with video, performance, and multimedia installations. “Theresa Hak Kyung Cha: Multiple Offerings” (organized by the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, and on through Nov. 21) is the first retrospective of Cha’s work in twenty-five years, and I can’t imagine a more beautiful curatorial vision. Everything about it—placement, context, sound, moving image—works to create a kind of holistic portrait of an artist who was as devoted to image as she was to language, and to show the ways in which each amplifies the other.

Indeed, her mysterious and uncategorizable book “Dictee,” from 1982, features a number of women talking, ranging from Joan of Arc to the artist’s mother, who lived through Japanese rule, when Korean could not be spoken in public. In “Dictee,” and in her performances, many of which are featured in “Multiple Offerings,” Cha’s and other women’s voices rise out of bodies that have lived through some form of oppression to come out on the other side as whole and true. One walks away from this historic show deeply moved by its singularity, and angry: in 1982, shortly before her first exhibition at Artists Space was scheduled to open, Cha, who was working on a series of photographs about her time employed at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, was murdered.—Hilton Als

Dance

The first part of “Adaku”—a dance-theatre trilogy by Okwui Okpokwasili and Peter Born that spools out a speculative vision rooted in a pre-colonial African village—ended with wailing, as a beloved daughter was caught up in the transatlantic slave trade. Part 2, “She Shivers with It,” which has its New York début at BAM, starts with that choral cry and fast-forwards into an alternate present, tapping into embodied memory to trace the lineage of the lost daughter. Amid two hundred feet of snaking red coil, the ritualistic performance lingers in pain but also mines the humor in a magical hairdresser.—Brian Seibert (BAM Fisher; Nov. 11-15.)

Dance

Paul Taylor Dance Company has lately diversified its repertory considerably. This season includes new and recent pieces by the resident artists Robert Battle and Lauren Lovette; an example of mid-century psychedelia by Alwin Nikolais; and “Messengers, Maidens and the End of Something Else,” by the jokey postmodernist Pam Tanowitz. A tongue-in-cheek exploration of the classical-music repertoire, the dance pairs the first and fourth movements of Schubert’s “Death and the Maiden” quartet with a bright palette of movement and color. Those who come for Taylor will be rewarded with rare revivals of “Arabesque,” from 1999, which is set to a Debussy composition that suggests prettiness but soon reveals something darker, and “Byzantium,” from 1984, which probes the degenerate sides of society.—Marina Harss (David H. Koch Theatre; through Nov. 22.)

Broadway

Molière collapsed onstage while performing the lead role of his last play, “The Imaginary Invalid,” and died hours later. That it’s a sendup of doctors and medicine is an irony worthy of its author. Brandon J. Dirden’s revival, for Roundabout, features Bill Irwin (who also adapted the text from Doug Skinner’s translation) as the lead: a perfectly healthy hypochondriac exploited by greedy, bullshitting physicians. Irwin’s performance is a marvel of physical and vocal comedy, complemented by Crystal A. Dickinson as his sweet-talking, gold-digging wife; Rachel Bloom as the sly servant who sees and fixes all; and a bloviating Brooks Ashmanskas, double-cast as two of the quacks. In its whirligig puncturing of pretense, this sumptuous production not only honors Molière’s spirit but makes it felt, offering us ninety minutes with him in comedy heaven.—Dan Stahl (Haimes; through Nov. 22.)

Off Broadway

In the new musical “Midnight,” Rail (Todrick Hall, who also wrote and directed), an enslaved Black man, falls in love with Richard (Jeremy Beloate), a white man he works for; in the second act, they swap social placements, so that Rail is the wealthy landowner and Richard the enslaved worker. (They remain in love.) Even if the songs go on twice as long as is necessary to the plot, the singing is a considerable pleasure, with Kennedy Caughell bringing a spirited assurance to her turn as Scarlet, an imperious Southern belle, while Charlotte Odusanya imbues Lily Rose—a young woman wooed by Rail’s “pretty eyes”—with a lambent sweetness. Hall’s ambitious show is concerned with racial legibility and manipulation, but he’s threading with a dull needle.—Rhoda Feng (DR2; through Jan. 3.)

Movies

Reappropriating the means of production after two elaborate movies, the director Kogonada filmed “Zi” in Hong Kong, shooting on the fly with a main cast of three and a scant crew to match. The results are as daring as the method; the title character, a Hong Kong-born violinist (Michelle Mao), is awaiting test results about a possible brain tumor. In a variation on Agnès Varda’s “Cléo from 5 to 7,” Zi has hallucinations—seeing flashes of her future self, as though mentally stuck in her own past—but a chance connection with an American wanderer (Haley Lu Richardson) and a Korean scientist (Jin Ha) offers hope: the trio’s lurching, passionate overnight ramble helps diagnose a metaphysical malady. The filmmaker’s ardently curious vision of the cityscape links inner lives to history, self-images to aesthetics.—Richard Brody (Metrograph through Nov. 15, and in limited release.)

Post-Punk

Since its inception, in 2019, the torrid band Sweeping Promises has been a project about the act of creating. Its partners, Lira Mondal and Caufield Schnug, started up on a whim when a jam sesh in an abandoned science lab conjured their first song, which became the title track for their 2020 début, “Hunger for a Way Out.” The band was imagined as a space beyond the duo’s other musical projects to “capture the exhilaration of writing songs in the moment,” as Mondal put it, and the music is governed primarily by impulses—it’s lo-fi and punk, possessing a free spirit and a resourceful nature. Their most recent album, “You Say I Romanticize,” reaffirms their core drive with songs more explicitly about committing to an artistic life.—Sheldon Pearce (Baby’s All Right; Nov. 11.)

Taran Dugal excavates cocktails in Bushwick.

Brooklyn night life is full of imposing figures: brutish bouncers, cool-kid carousers, the rare haughty bartender. But it wasn’t until this summer’s opening of the Museum, a low-lit cocktail lounge in Bushwick, that barflies had to contend with a T. rex—or, at least, a replica of one, whose skull is mounted on a table in the back room. On a recent weekend, three friends sat to the dino’s right, trying their best to ignore his unmistakable glower. They’d begun their evening in the Gift Shop, a cozy parlor up front serving drinks and finger foods, before making their way through the establishment’s Exhibition Hall, a narrow space lined with engraved skulls, Egyptian figurines, and a kaleidoscopic array of gemstones and crystals. In the back, the friends perused the menu, which consisted of cocktails inspired by different aspects of natural history. The most adventurous of the group ordered the Insectarium, an earthy honey-gin Negroni with a cricket-infused tincture, accompanied by a small piece of ant-ridden chocolate. The queasiest, looking away, opted for the Crystal Pass, a velvety Old-Fashioned incorporating oaky Scotch, bourbon, and mole sauce. The third friend, between sips of his Birds of the World (a tangy tequila-based concoction of elderflower, sunflower seeds, guava, and pineapple), began eavesdropping on a couple nearby, whose discussion had turned to mammalian politics. “Hyenas get a bad rep from ‘The Lion King,’ ” a man said to his date, “but they’re just kind of taking care of the leftovers, you know?” The eavesdropper, busy finishing a delectable pepper-chicken skewer, couldn’t agree more. Eventually, the place emptied out, and the trio took their leave to the hazy groove of a Khruangbin track. After all, the sun had set, the T. rex was still glowering, and one can never be too careful in a museum at night.

P.S. Good stuff on the internet:

  • Seven generations of broom making
  • Tom Hiddleston says: close the toes
  • “Like a hug in a dish”

  • What it’s like to be consumed by obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Brian Seibert has been contributing to The New Yorker since 2002. He is the author of “What the Eye Hears: A History of Tap Dancing,” which won an Anisfield-Wolf Book Award. His writing appears in the New York Times and the New York Review of Books. A Guggenheim fellow, he teaches at Yale University.

Dan Stahl is a member of The New Yorker’s editorial staff.

Rhoda Feng, who received the 2025 Nona Balakian Citation for Excellence in Reviewing, has also written about theatre and books for Artforum, the Boston Globe, and the Times Literary Supplement, among other publications.

Sheldon Pearce is a music writer for The New Yorker’s Goings On newsletter.

Taran Dugal is a member of The New Yorker’s editorial staff.

title: A Cartoonist’s Depiction of the Moment Things Got Weird
author: @NewYorker
content:
As a kid, Chris Ware loved collecting and preserving comics. He graduated from buying Batman and Superman at the nearby 7-Eleven to honing his taste at the local comic shop, where he revelled in the walls of comics, the smell of self-destructing woodpulp, and the polypropylene bags that protected his newfound treasures. That love of the physical object led the adult cartoonist to produce his own semi-regular experimental periodical, The Acme Novelty Library, whose serialized stories were later collected in hardcover graphic novels that bookstores were happy to misfile in their children’s sections.

When “Life Is Complicated,” a retrospective of Ware’s original drawings, finished touring museums in Europe and was about to land in Columbus, Ohio, at the Billy Ireland Cartoon Library & Museum for its only American stop, the artist didn’t want it to arrive without a printed souvenir. He returned to the traditional comic book, an ambition that soon metastasized into three comic books, a Sunday-sized comic section, and a cardboard model of a contemporary office building, all housed in a (compostable) keepsake box. Like “Building Stories” (2012), this twenty-first issue of Acme asks the reader to take the lead. Its three twenty-four-page booklets excerpt longer works that he told me he has been writing since the coronavirus pandemic began. This old-fashioned format delivers a thoroughly modern reading experience, one that parallels the disruptions of those years and the unravelling of reality we’ve endured since 2016. Shifts in scale allude to the fractal nature of the narrative, and characters and story lines make cameo appearances from booklet to booklet. It’s interactive in the truest sense: the reader, aware that she is building her own story, creates her own linearity and discovers her own rhymes, echoes, and harmonies.

In the pages below, excerpted from the broadsheet-size “Untitled,” Ware chronicles the end of the world and the disruptions brought on by the pandemic. “The vogue for baking, ukulele, and homes as places to actually live in rather than just come home to reflected a shift, however temporarily, to what really matters in life. It also seems to me to be the moment when everything started to feel really weird,” Ware told me.
